transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
The Senate has passed a permitting bill, NPR's Julia Simon reports on the Bipartisan
American Affordability and Jobs Act, which has split Democrats and environmentalists.
The bill comes down to permitting.
Proponents of the bill say that the current permitting process is outdated, inefficient,
and needs updates.
That is easing of environmental regulations and changes to laws around building electrical
transmission lines.
Some climate change advocates say the bill will allow the country to build more solar,
wind, and battery projects.
And many climate scientists do agree that the U.S. needs to speed up building renewable
energy projects and transmission lines.
But other Democratic lawmakers oppose the bill.
They argue it will worsen climate pollution by also making it easier to greenlight oil
and gas projects and energy-hungry data centers.
And they say it will weaken protections for clean air and water.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
After Ukraine strikes on a bridge connecting Russia to Russian-occupied Crimea, President
Vladimir Putin says he will not negotiate any cease-fires covering energy infrastructure.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports that Ukrainians are preparing for retaliation.
Russian drones are targeting Kiev, and air raid sirens wailed most of the day.
Explosions and the sound of air defense fire rang out across the city.
NPR recorded the explosions while sheltering inside its bureau.
At least one person was killed, and many buildings are damaged, including the Austrian and Dutch
embassies.
In a post on social media, Ukraine's foreign minister urges the international community
to condemn Russia's "terror" in the boldest terms.
President Trump, meanwhile, was meeting with Vladimir Putin in China, where he greeted
him warmly, calling him "my friend."
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kiev.
President Trump is back from his trip to Asia and says he will hold a press conference at
the White House Friday to discuss the trip.
On Thursday, leaders from Ukraine and nearly 40 other delegations met in Berlin in a show
of support for Ukraine.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta served chipmaker Invidia with an investigative subpoena.
The subpoena follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang following an affair with a woman
who may have spied for China, impures John Ruich reports.
The California AG's office says in a statement it's asking Invidia whether its advanced chips
or confidential information may have gone to China, and whether Invidia misled investors
and the public.
Bonta says the conduct of the company and former CEO Jensen Huang raises red flags.
Huang stepped down last week after admitting to an extramarital affair.
U.S. intelligence services believe one of the women had ties to a Chinese spy agency.
Huang had been a vocal opponent of U.S. export controls that banned certain high-end chips
from being exported to China.
John Ruich, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News.
El Nino-driven storms have been slamming California this week, causing flooding in cities, including
San Francisco.
Member Station KQED Ezra David Romero reports on streets turned into rivers and cars floating
in flood water.
San Francisco's mostly flat mission district was hit hard by the rain on Wednesday.
Rich Deliah armored his bagel shop, Bagueleta, with a metal flood wall.
But water still spilled out of every drain and toilet in his shop.
He says it ruined the rebuild he completed just a few years back.
We have machines, mixers, ovens, obviously with the water there, we didn't really want
to plug anything in and see for Earth.
While he's nervous about a storm this weekend and a potential atmospheric river next week,
he's even more worried about how El Nino could cause a wetter than average winter for California.
For NPR News, I'm Ezra David Romero in San Francisco.
Heavy rain and the potential for flash flooding are expected to continue into Friday and Florida,
where storms brought record rains to South Florida this week.
Forecasters warned of the potential for the storms to move toward the Carolinas and the
Mid-Atlantic this weekend.
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic posted the biggest initial public offering
on Record Thursday.
The company's shares surged at one point, topping $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic was welcomed by Wall Street despite investor anxiety about an AI bubble, AI-related
stocks, contributing to a slide in Asian shares after U.S. stocks posted losses.
I'm Giles Snyder.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Senate passes permitting bill easing environmental rules and transmission line changes, splitting Democrats and environmentalists
Putin rejects energy infrastructure cease-fires after Ukrainian strike on Crimea bridge; Kyiv hit by Russian drones
President Trump returns from Asia trip, meets Putin in China, plans White House press conference Friday
Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenas Nvidia over CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and possible China spy ties
El Nino storms flood California cities including San Francisco's Mission District, threatening businesses like Bagueleta
Heavy rain and flash flood threat continue in Florida, with storms possibly moving toward Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic
AI company Anthropic posts largest-ever initial public offering, shares topping $2 trillion valuation at one point
